subChunks.title: CREATE VIEW and Materialized Views
subChunks.hookHtml: Views are named, reusable queries stored in the database. They let you hide complexity, enforce access control, and present data in shapes that match your application's needs.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
CREATE VIEW

CREATE VIEW active_apprentices AS
SELECT a.id, a.name, a.xp, m.name AS mentor
FROM   apprentices AS a
LEFT JOIN mentors AS m ON a.mentor_id = m.id
WHERE a.rank != 'Novice';

-- Use the view like a table:
SELECT * FROM active_apprentices WHERE xp > 1000;

-- Update the view definition:
CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW active_apprentices AS ...;

-- Drop it:
DROP VIEW active_apprentices;

What views are and are not

  • A view is a stored query — not a stored copy of data
  • Every time you SELECT from a view, the underlying query runs
  • Views do not improve performance on their own (unless the engine can push conditions down)

Updatable views

Simple single-table views can be updated (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE) if they have no aggregates, DISTINCT, GROUP BY, UNION, or LIMIT. Most complex views are read-only.

Materialized views (PostgreSQL)

CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW monthly_xp AS
SELECT DATE_TRUNC('month', completed_at) AS month,
       SUM(xp_reward) AS total_xp
FROM   quest_completions
JOIN   quests ON quests.id = quest_completions.quest_id
GROUP BY 1;

-- Refresh when underlying data changes:
REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW monthly_xp;
REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY monthly_xp;  -- no read lock

A materialized view stores the result set. It is fast to query but stale until refreshed. The CONCURRENTLY option allows reads during refresh but requires a UNIQUE index.

storyBeats.text: Twelve reports query the same complex five-table JOIN. A change in business logic means changing all twelve queries.

storyBeats.speaker: Cipher the Archivist
storyBeats.text: A view encapsulates a query behind a name. Change the view definition and all twelve reports update automatically. The view does not store data — each query runs the underlying SELECT fresh. A materialized view does store data and is fast to query, but you must refresh it when the underlying tables change.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
📜 View design

Describe the view you would create to expose this query as leaderboard, and explain when you would use a materialized view instead of a regular view for leaderboard data:

SELECT a.name, a.rank, SUM(qc.score) AS total_score,
       COUNT(qc.id) AS quests_completed
FROM   apprentices AS a
LEFT JOIN quest_completions AS qc ON qc.apprentice_id = a.id
GROUP BY a.name, a.rank
ORDER BY total_score DESC NULLS LAST;
subChunks.guidedPracticeModelAnswer:
Regular view:
CREATE VIEW leaderboard AS
SELECT a.name, a.rank, SUM(qc.score) AS total_score, COUNT(qc.id) AS quests_completed
FROM   apprentices AS a
LEFT JOIN quest_completions AS qc ON qc.apprentice_id = a.id
GROUP BY a.name, a.rank
ORDER BY total_score DESC NULLS LAST;

Use a regular view when: data freshness is critical (every page load shows current data) and the underlying query is fast enough.

Use a materialized view when: the leaderboard query is expensive (many rows, complex aggregation) and a few minutes of staleness is acceptable. Schedule REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY hourly or daily. Users get fast reads; the refresh happens in the background.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml:
🏹 Solo

Explain three use cases where a view is the right tool: (1) security, (2) abstraction, (3) backward compatibility during schema migration.
subChunks.modelAnswer:
(1) Security: Grant users SELECT on a view that exposes only non-sensitive columns (e.g. name, rank) while the underlying table has salary, email, etc. Users query the view and never see the hidden columns.

(2) Abstraction: A complex five-table JOIN is exposed as a view named 'order_summary'. Application code queries the view. When the underlying schema changes, only the view definition changes — application SQL remains stable.

(3) Backward compatibility: When renaming a table or column, keep the old name as a view that maps to the new name. Old queries continue to work during a migration period.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain the difference between a regular view and a materialized view. When would you choose each one?

options: A stored SELECT query that behaves like a table — the query runs each time the view is accessed
A copy of query results stored for fast access
A backup of a table at a point in time
questions.answer: A stored SELECT query that behaves like a table — the query runs each time the view is accessed
questions.explanation: A regular view is a named query. There is no stored data — every SELECT against the view executes the underlying query fresh. A materialized view is different: it caches the result.

questions.prompt: When is a view updatable (supports INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE)?
options: When the view queries a single table with no aggregates, DISTINCT, GROUP BY, UNION, or LIMIT
When the view has a primary key column
When the view is created with CREATE UPDATABLE VIEW
questions.answer: When the view queries a single table with no aggregates, DISTINCT, GROUP BY, UNION, or LIMIT
questions.explanation: Simple single-table views without row-collapsing operations can be made updatable. The engine translates the DML on the view into the equivalent DML on the underlying table. Complex views (joins, aggregates) are read-only.

questions.prompt: What does `REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY` do compared to plain `REFRESH`?
options: Allows reads on the materialized view during the refresh — requires a UNIQUE index on the view
Refreshes only the rows that changed
Runs the refresh asynchronously in the background
Locks the view exclusively during the refresh for faster writes
questions.answer: Allows reads on the materialized view during the refresh — requires a UNIQUE index on the view
questions.explanation: Plain REFRESH acquires an exclusive lock — queries block during refresh. CONCURRENTLY uses a diff algorithm to update the view without blocking reads. It requires a UNIQUE index on the materialized view to identify rows.

questions.prompt: A reporting query takes 30 seconds on 100M rows. The report is viewed by 500 users concurrently. What is the best solution?
options: Materialized view refreshed hourly — fast reads, acceptable 1-hour staleness for a report
Regular view — all 500 queries run the 30-second query simultaneously
Add more indexes to the base tables
Cache the results in application code
questions.answer: Materialized view refreshed hourly — fast reads, acceptable 1-hour staleness for a report
questions.explanation: 500 concurrent 30-second queries = 15,000 seconds of database time per refresh cycle. A materialized view computes once per hour, stores the result, and serves all 500 users in milliseconds. Application-level caching works too but materialized views are database-native and always consistent with the refresh.
